objectClass: posixGroup
dn: cn=team,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: groupOfNames
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -o ldif-wrap=no -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(|(uid=*)(cn=*))' dn objectClass description sshPublicKey
dn: uid=dave,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: person
objectClass: organizationalPerson
objectClass: inetOrgPerson
objectClass: uidObject
dn: cn=staff,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: posixGroup

dave has lost ldapPublicKey and with it his sshPublicKey (not in AUX),and his description (NOT). erin is gone (MUST telephoneNumber), and so isteam: it has no gidNumber, so it is a groupOfNames, and no structure rule places a groupOfNames under ou=groups. That last one is the tree’s rule applied to data, which the next section explains.

What the structure rules do to the tree

With at least one active DIT structure rule, authnd walks the tree it will publish, at startup and in check:

  • the suffix (base_dn), given the class its RDN names: dc adomain, o an organization, ou an organizationalUnit, c acountry, l a locality. A suffix named by any other attribute is refused;
  • ou=people and ou=groups, as organizationalUnits;
  • the RDN attribute authnd names its people by (uid) and its groups by (cn).

A container no rule places, a suffix of a kind no rule has a name form for, a name form that refuses uid or cn, or a container under which nothing authnd publishes could be placed, refuses startup, and check: every refusal at once, naming the DN, the rule or name form and the clause, and never echoing a secret. A person or group whose structural class depends on its data (an sn,a gidNumber) and has no rule under its container is left out and said instead, as team was above: the server starts. With no active structure rule,nothing changes.

A schema whose only structure rule for people, peopleByCN, places a name form that wants cn (accountByCN: OC account MUST cn):

$ authnd check cases/bad.hcl
authnd: DIT structure rules: authnd names its people uid=<name>,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org, and an account named so is refused: the RDN (uid) is allowed by the name form of no DIT structure rule that places account under an entry governed by the rule 2: accountByCN needs cn

authnd names its people uid=<name>: the rules have to allow it. And a schema whose rule for organizationalUnit has no SUP, so that anorganizationalUnit can only be at the root, leaves both ou=people andou=groups without a place, and says both at once:

$ authnd check cases/root.hcl
authnd: DIT structure rules: ou=people,dc=example,dc=org, where authnd publishes its people, as an organizationalUnit: no DIT structure rule allows organizationalUnit under an entry governed by the rule suffix (X.501 13.7.5)
DIT structure rules: ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org, where authnd publishes its groups, as an organizationalUnit: no DIT structure rule allows organizationalUnit under an entry governed by the rule suffix (X.501 13.7.5)

Both exit with status 1. The files behind them (cases/bad.schema andcases/root.schema) hold the same five name forms and only the structure rules that make the point.

Where authnd and slapd differ

go-authn/ldap reads the OpenLDAP files, and some of the rules are OpenLDAP’s.These are the differences, said rather than discovered:

  • slapd implements content rules only. It has no directive for name forms or structure rules. Format writes nameform and ditstructurerule keywords, which are this library’s, and slapd refuses them: keep those in the HCL, or in a file only authnd reads. ditcontentrule is slapd’s.
  • An OBSOLETE rule is inactive (RFC 4512 §4.1.6), as is its name form or structure rule. slapd refuses the entry instead.
  • Without a content rule, auxiliary classes are allowed. That is slapd’s behaviour (its SLAP_DISALLOW_AUX_WO_CR flag is set by no disallow keyword), and authnd’s. RFC 4512 §2.4.3 says otherwise; the library offers it as ValidateOptions{StrictAuxiliary: true}, and authnd does not set it.
  • libldap cannot read a structure rule’s SUP. A structure rule with aSUP is read here and not by libldap, so libldap’s refusal of such a file is not a verdict on the file.
  • A file that redefines a rule is refused, even word for word, like every other definition (above).

What it costs

Measured on 2026-10-30 with BenchmarkPublish10k (go-authn/authnd,rules_bench_test.go, -cpu 1) on authnd v0.13.3, which embeds go-authn/ldap v0.11.3: publishing 10,000 people makes 97 allocations per entry with the rules of testdata/rules.schema and 69 without (v0.13.2: 128 and 85; v0.13.0: 416 and 265), and a run takes 42.6 MiB with the rules and 25.7 MiB without (v0.13.2: 54.8 and 33.7; v0.13.0: 147.5 and 88.0). This includes dropping a precluded description and validating again.The times, about 66 ms against 36 ms, are the median of five interleaved runs at a load of 4.8: the rules still cost about 1.8 times as much. The second validation that dropping the description requires and the structure rules’ second read of the DN are among the largest parts of the difference that were attributed.

Upgrading

Nothing changes for a schema without rules: v0.12.4 refused all three kinds, so a configuration that started on it holds none. There is one exception. Aschema { } string that is not valid UTF-8 (an overlong encoding HCL lets through) started on v0.12.4 and is refused now, because it could not be published as it was written.

SUPANN, as the real example

SUPANN is the attribute set of French higher education and research(supannPerson, supannEtablissement, supannEntite…), with eduPerson beside it. RENATER publishes the technical schema, with the others, on its documentation page:

https://services.renater.fr/documentation/supann/supann2021/recommandations/tables_references/schemas_techniques_supann

Download the file from there. It is not reproduced on this site: it states no licence, so this page does not copy it, and a copy here would go stale when RENATER revises it. Then:

sudo install -o root -g authnd -m 0640 supann.schema eduperson.ldif /etc/authnd/
schema_files = ["/etc/authnd/supann.schema", "/etc/authnd/eduperson.ldif"]

users "sql" {
 # ...
 users_attributes = "select login, sn, etab as \"supannEtablissement\" from staff"
 object_classes = ["supannPerson", "eduPerson"]
 group_object_classes = ["supannGroupe"]
}

Run authnd check and read the schema: lines first: a file that slapd loads loads here, and one that redefines a standard definition is refused with its line. Then read the published without lines: a person lacking a MUST of supannPerson or eduPerson is published without the class, andcheck names the MUST. Quote an alias where its spelling matters(PostgreSQL lower-cases an unquoted one; seethe entries).

About the transcripts

Every command on this page was run again on 2026-10-26 with the v0.12.3 release binary (authnd-darwin-arm64, checked against SHA256SUMS; go version -m: go1.27.3, mod github.com/go-authn/authnd v0.12.3, vcs.modified=false) and OpenLDAP’s ldapsearch, on 127.0.0.1, in a scratch directory, with the files shown. The paths are relative for that reason; a service uses absolute ones. The schema is an example written for this page.

The section on DIT content rules, name forms and DIT structure rules was run on 2026-10-26 with the v0.13.0 release binary (authnd-darwin-arm64, checked by relverify against SHA256SUMS and its attestation; go version -m: go1.27.3, mod github.com/go-authn/authnd v0.13.0; authnd --version: authnd version v0.13.0), OpenLDAP’s ldapsearch and ldapschema built from the go-authn/ldap v0.11.0 tag (go install, go1.27.1; it has no release binary). Every output there was printed by those programs, in a scratch directory, on 127.0.0.1; the files behind the transcripts are shown or described beside them.

item.title: check, before you restart something people log in through
item.description:
authnd check /etc/authnd
authnd check --config a.hcl --config b.hcl

check reads the configuration exactly as the server does, opens everything the server opens before it listens — the files, the database,the directory behind this one, the identity provider’s discovery document,the TLS certificate and key, the keytab — and prints what would be published and to whom, without listening. It prints where every credential comes from and never what is in it. It exits 0 and ends with this configuration can be served, or exits 1 with the one sentence that stops the server.

A configuration that can be served

Two user blocks, a reader, and a SQLite database, in a directory of two files (authnd.hcl and people.hcl):

$ authnd check etc/authnd
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
bob the configuration file an NT hash account, uidObject uid
dora a sqlite database a password account, uidObject uid
eli a sqlite database an NT hash account, uidObject uid
GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS
engineers dora and eli groupOfNames
staff alice, bob and dora groupOfNames
alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
dora has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
eli has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
group engineers has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid)
group staff has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid)
a bind carries a password
bob and eli cannot bind with a password: their sources hold only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against
cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

Reading it

The first line is the scheme, the address and the base: ldap://,ldaps://, or ldap+starttls:// — see TLS.

column
FROM the source that owns the name: the configuration file, a sqlite database (or postgres, mysql), or the url of a directory behind this one
CAN PROVE a password (held, so it can be compared and keys derived from it), a password check (another directory answers yes or no), an NT hash, N keys, a one-time-code secret, or nothing
PUBLISHED AS the entry’s object classes, without top, as the shapes give them — or NOT PUBLISHED (see below) for an entry that fails the schema
WITH the attributes the entry carries, read off the entry a search returns: uid; cn wherever a class allows it; what the sources gave, less what was dropped; sshPublicKey when there are keys; sambaSID and sambaNTPassword when publish_nt_hash is on and the person has an NT key and a SID

The group table has a PUBLISHED AS column too: posixGroup,groupOfNames or organizationalRole. Up to v0.10.2, PUBLISHED AS was the list of attributes, uid and cn for nearly everybody, and there was noWITH column.

The lines after the tables say what a person needs to know before relying on the configuration. First, about the entries:

  • who is not a posixAccount, and which of uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory they lack;
  • which groups have no gidNumber, and what they are published as instead;
  • every attribute dropped because no class of its entry allows it, and which classes would;
  • every entry not published, with each problem the schema check found;
  • who has an NT key and no sambaSID, and so no sambaNTPassword.

From v0.12.0, between the first line and the tables, what asite schema added, and what the sources declare:

  • the schema files and schema blocks loaded, and what each adds:schema: etc/authnd/example.schema adds 3 object identifier macros, 2 attribute types and 2 object classes;
  • the classes each source declares: users "sql" declares exampleStaff and exampleLockerHolder for its people, with the position of the declaration;
  • every class left off a person or group, because it lacks a MUST of a class its source declares: ben is published without exampleStaff, which its source declares: ben has no exampleEmployeeId, which exampleStaff requires, and, after the attributes’ lines, those it took with it;
  • a group for which two sources declare different classes: the first source’s list is published and the second’s ignored.

A file that does not build, a redefinition, and a declared class that is undefined, STRUCTURAL or one authnd derives stop check and the server alike, with the file or configuration position.

Then, about binds and searches:

  • what a bind carries: a password, or, with an mfa block,a password with a 6-digit code after it; with an oidc block,where tokens come from and over what;
  • who cannot bind with a password at all: people known only by an NT hash — see people;
  • who may search: the readers, or no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected;
  • whether sambaNTPassword is published, and over what — seepublish_nt_hash;
  • with a kerberos block, the realm andwho can and who cannot be issued a ticket, with the reason;
  • with an mfa block, who has no second factor, and so cannot bind with a password; with an oidc block beside it the line adds that a token whoseamr names two kinds still can;
  • a group that names somebody no source has.

That last one is published as it stands — a front for one system legitimately carries names another one owns — but it is said, because the other reading is a typo. In a posixGroup the stranger is a memberUid; in a groupOfNames it is a member DN that names no entry here,member: uid=zoe,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org here, which go-authn/directory’sldapdir from v0.14.0 maps to nobody. Here the database’s team_members table has a row for zoe, who is nobody here:

GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS
engineers dora, eli and zoe groupOfNames
staff alice, bob and dora groupOfNames
[...]
engineers names zoe, who has no entry here: the group is published as it stands, and nothing here can prove them

(A group block naming a stranger is refused outright; seepeople.)

What it refuses

Each of these stops check and the server alike, with exit status 1. They are on the pages where they belong; a few, as printed:

$ authnd check cases/nobody.hcl
authnd: there is nobody here: name a user, or a users block reading a database or a directory
$ authnd check cases/nthash-clear.hcl
authnd: publish_nt_hash needs cert_file and key_file: an NT hash IS the credential, and 0.0.0.0:3893 is not loopback, so it would cross a network in the clear
$ authnd check cases/krb-mfa.hcl
authnd: kerberos and mfa together: the mfa block asks every bind for a password AND a code, and a kinit carries only the password -- this KDC has no second-factor pre-authentication, so a realm here would accept one factor where the mfa block demands two. Remove one of the blocks
$ authnd check empty
authnd: empty has no .hcl files in it
$ authnd
authnd: no configuration: give a .hcl file or a directory of them

The certificate, the keytab, and the one thing it cannot see

A certificate that does not load and a keytab without krbtgt/REALM are refused by check, in the words the server would use:

$ authnd check cases/badcert
authnd: the certificate: open tls/missing.pem: no such file or directory
$ authnd check cases/nokrbtgt
authnd: kdc: the keytab has no krbtgt key for this realm: matching key not found in keytab. Looking for "krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG" realm: EXAMPLE.ORG kvno: 0 etype: 18

What check cannot know without listening is whether the ports are free. A second server on the same Kerberos address passes check and is refused at start:

$ authnd --config cases/realm2
authnd: kerberos udp 127.0.0.1:18388: listen udp 127.0.0.1:18388: bind: address already in use

Run it as the service account 

sudo -u authnd authnd check /etc/authnd

so that a file only root can read fails here, not at the restart. Run it with the new binary before an upgrade; see install.

item.title: TLS: ldaps:// or StartTLS, and not both at once
item.description:
listen = "0.0.0.0:636"
cert_file = "/etc/authnd/cert.pem" # the chain, leaf first
key_file = "/etc/authnd/key.pem"

cert_file and key_file together turn TLS on; one without the other is refused (one without the other serves nothing). TLS 1.2 is the minimum.authnd has no ACME client: the two files are written by something else —go-authn/servercert, certbot, a site’s own CA — and authnd is restarted after each renewal,because the certificate is read once, when the listener opens.

Two ways, one listener each

starttls the listener check says
ldaps:// not set the TLS handshake happens before a byte of LDAP is spoken ldaps://…
StartTLS starttls = true plaintext, upgraded when the client asks (RFC 4511 §4.14) ldap+starttls://…

It is one or the other and has to be: a listener cannot both require a handshake and wait to see whether one is asked for. Which one a site wants is about its clients: ldaps:// on 636 is what most of them are configured for, and StartTLS is what a client pointed at 389 with “use TLS” ticked will ask for. A site that needs both runs two instances, each with its own--config. starttls = true without a certificate is refused:

$ authnd check cases/starttls-nocert.hcl
authnd: starttls needs cert_file and key_file: there is nothing to upgrade a connection WITH

ldaps://

The server, a CA-signed certificate for 127.0.0.1, and the chain verified by a client that is not this program:

$ authnd --config ldaps
ldaps on 127.0.0.1:3636, serving 3 people from the configuration file
uid=carol,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org is published without sambaNTPassword: no sambaSID and no uidNumber to derive one from
$ openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:3636 -CAfile tls/ca.pem -verify_return_error -verify_ip 127.0.0.1 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'Verify return|Protocol|subject=|issuer='
subject=CN=localhost
issuer=CN=docs test CA
Protocol: TLSv1.3
Verify return code: 0 (ok)
Protocol : TLSv1.3
Verify return code: 0 (ok)

StartTLS, which refuses until it is asked for

StartTLS is requested by the client, so merely offering it promises nothing: a client that never asks would bind in the clear. A listener withstarttls = true therefore refuses every bind and every search until the connection has been upgraded, with confidentialityRequired:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=bob)'
ldap_bind: Confidentiality required (13)
additional info: this listener requires TLS, and nothing asked for it
$ LDAPTLS_REQCERT=never ldapsearch -ZZ -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=bob)'
dn: uid=bob,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: account
objectClass: sambaSamAccount
objectClass: uidObject
uid: bob
cn: bob
sambaSID: S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330-1104
sambaNTPassword: 8846F7EAEE8FB117AD06BDD830B7586C

(-ZZ is “StartTLS, and fail if it fails”. LDAPTLS_REQCERT=never is there because the ldapsearch macOS ships trusts the system store and could not be told to trust this test CA; the chain was checked separately withopenssl s_client -starttls ldap -CAfile tls/ca.pem -verify_return_error,which answered Verify return code: 0 (ok).)

That refusal is what makes cert_file a guarantee rather than an offer — and it is what publish_nt_hash relies on. It includes the anonymous bindldapsearch -x sends before reading the root DSE, so on a StartTLS listener that discovery query, too, needs -ZZ.

publish_nt_hash

sambaNTPassword is what lets a Samba or another SMB server authenticate people through this directory, and it is not a password hash in the sense a login form means: whoever holds MD4(UTF16LE(password)) authenticates as that person over NTLMv2 without ever learning the password. So it is published only when asked for, and, from v0.11.0, with the domain the people’s SIDs belong to:

publish_nt_hash = true
samba {
 domain_sid = "S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330" # `net getlocalsid` on the SMB server
}

Asking for it is refused unless the listener has TLS, or is loopback(127.0.0.0/8, ::1, localhost) and so on no network at all:

$ authnd check cases/nthash-clear.hcl
authnd: publish_nt_hash needs cert_file and key_file: an NT hash IS the credential, and 0.0.0.0:3893 is not loopback, so it would cross a network in the clear

The samba block

sambaNTPassword belongs to Samba’s sambaSamAccount, whose MUST is uid and sambaSID, and no other class allows it. Every entry authnd publishes passes the schema it serves, so the attribute is published only on a sambaSamAccount, and that needs a SID:

key
domain_sid required: the SMB server’s domain SID, S-1-5-21-…, as net getlocalsid prints it
algorithmic_rid_base optional, 1000 by default, Samba’s. An odd number, or one below 1000, is refused: Samba would silently use another one

A person’s sambaSID is their own sambaSID attribute when a source gives one (attributes).Otherwise it is domain_sid-RID, with RID = 2 × uidNumber +algorithmic_rid_base: Samba’s algorithmic mapping (smb.conf(5),algorithmic rid base). A person with an NT key and neither is publishedwithout sambaNTPassword, and check and the startup log say who. The Samba definitions are added to the schema served at cn=Subschema only when the block is there; they were written from Samba’s published OIDs, names and syntaxes, not copied from its GPL-3.0 samba.schema.

Breaking for v0.10.x configurations: publish_nt_hash without a samba block does not start

v0.10.x served publish_nt_hash = true alone. From v0.11.0 that configuration is refused at startup and by check, with what to add:

$ authnd check cases/nthash.hcl
authnd: publish_nt_hash needs a samba block: sambaNTPassword belongs to Samba's sambaSamAccount, whose MUST is uid and sambaSID, and a SID needs the domain's. Add
samba {
domain_sid = "S-1-5-21-..." # the SMB server's: `net getlocalsid` prints it
}
and each person's sambaSID is their own sambaSID attribute, or domain_sid-(2 x uidNumber + 1000), Samba's algorithmic mapping; `authnd check` lists who has neither

Run check with the new binary before upgrading. Refusing is deliberate:the v0.10.x entry cannot pass the schema, and the two quiet alternatives —dropping the attribute, which takes SMB away from everybody, or dropping the entry, which takes the person away — would both happen with nothing on the console.

A samba block without publish_nt_hash is refused too, since it would publish nothing:

$ authnd check cases/samba-alone.hcl
authnd: a samba block without publish_nt_hash publishes nothing: it is the domain of the sambaSID that sambaNTPassword needs. Remove it, or set publish_nt_hash = true

What check says

Three people on an ldaps:// listener: alice has a password and the POSIX trio, so their SID is derived (2 × 1000 + 1000); bob has only an NT hash and a sambaSID of their own; carol has a password and neither.

listen = "127.0.0.1:3636"
base_dn = "dc=example,dc=org"
cert_file = "tls/cert.pem"
key_file = "tls/key.pem"

publish_nt_hash = true
samba {
 domain_sid = "S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330"
}

reader "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" { password_file = "etc/authnd/reader.pw" }

user "alice" {
 password_file = "etc/authnd/alice.pw"
 attributes = { uidNumber = "1000", gidNumber = "1000", homeDirectory = "/home/alice" }
}

user "bob" {
 nt_hash = "8846F7EAEE8FB117AD06BDD830B7586C"
 attributes = { sambaSID = "S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330-1104" }
}

user "carol" { password = "carol-pw" }
$ authnd check ldaps
ldaps://127.0.0.1:3636, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password account, posixAccount, sambaSamAccount, uidObject uid, cn, gidNumber, homeDirectory, uidNumber, sambaSID and sambaNTPassword
bob the configuration file an NT hash account, sambaSamAccount, uidObject uid, cn, sambaSID and sambaNTPassword
carol the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, sambaSamAccount, uidObject
carol has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
carol is published without sambaNTPassword: no sambaSID and no uidNumber to derive one from
a bind carries a password
bob cannot bind with a password: the source holds only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against
cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not
sambaNTPassword is published over TLS: it IS the credential, and whoever reads it authenticates as that person over NTLMv2
in sambaSamAccount, with sambaSIDs in S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330 (a person's own sambaSID, or RID 2 x uidNumber + 1000)
this configuration can be served

and, for the StartTLS listener, sambaNTPassword is published over TLS, once StartTLS has been asked for. alice has no NT hash written down; theirs is derived from the password they have. bob’s hash is published for an SMB server to use, and check says, too, that bob cannot bind to authnd itself.carol’s entry is published without the attribute, and an SMB server cannot serve carol until a source gives them a uidNumber or a sambaSID.

What a reader is given, over the StartTLS listener of the same people:

$ LDAPTLS_REQCERT=never ldapsearch -ZZ -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=alice)'
dn: uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: account
objectClass: posixAccount
objectClass: sambaSamAccount
objectClass: uidObject
uid: alice
cn: alice
gidNumber: 1000
homeDirectory: /home/alice
uidNumber: 1000
sambaSID: S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330-3000
sambaNTPassword: D061EF15E9494B458016FA760CECDD63

Only a reader can search, so only a reader ever sees the attribute. Who may read it is therefore the same question as who holds a reader’s password.

NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and nothing else will do

A file server asking authnd about somebody can serve them over SMB only if the source held enough for that: a password, or the hash. A person who comes from a directory that only checks passwords — a password check incheck — can never be given a sambaNTPassword, whatever authnd does in between. Without publish_nt_hash, nobody can: check then sayssambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session.

Tokens need it too

An oidc block refuses a token over a connection that is not encrypted, unless allow_plaintext = true says that TLS is terminated in front of this process.

item.title: A person changing their own password
item.description:
A person may change their own password, and nobody else’s, through the RFC 3062 password modify operation (what ldappasswd sends) or an RFC 4511 modify. In both, the current password must be sent with the new one,whatever the connection bound with. A session bound with anOAUTHBEARER token — short-lived, and possibly one factor — could otherwise turn it into a permanent password that also works for kinit.

This is OpenLDAP’s ppolicy behaviour with pwdSafeModify set, with the result codes its ppolicy.c returns. RFC 3062 §3 allows it: “If oldPasswd is not present, the server MAY use other policy to determine whether or not to change the password.”

With ldappasswd

-t is a file holding the old password, -T one holding the new; -A and-S prompt for them instead.

$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -T alice.new
Result: Insufficient access (50)
Additional info: a password change must send the old password with the new one
$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -t wrong.pwin -T alice.new
Result: Server is unwilling to perform (53)
Additional info: the old password sent is not the current one
$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -t alice.pwin -T alice.new
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.new
dn:uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org

The old password stops working at once, for a bind and — with arealm —for kinit. The server says so in its output:

alice's password change was refused: the old password did not verify: directory: wrong password
alice changed their own password

authnd does not generate a password: a request without a new one is refused with unwillingToPerform (this server does not generate passwords: send the one you want). A password it invented would have to be sent back over the connection, and the one place it is certain to end up is a terminal’s scrollback.

With ldapmodify

The change is a delete of the old value followed by an add of the new one, in one request. RFC 4511 §4.6 applies a modify’s changes in order and atomically, so the delete — and the whole request with it — fails unless the value deleted is the one held:

dn: uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
changetype: modify
delete: userPassword
userPassword: alice-test-pw
-
add: userPassword
userPassword: alice-new-pw
-

A bare replace proves nothing, and anything but userPassword is not something this server changes:

$ ldapmodify -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -f replace.ldif
ldap_modify: Insufficient access (50)
additional info: a password change must send the old password with the new one
modifying entry "uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org"
$ ldapmodify -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -f other.ldif
ldap_modify: Server is unwilling to perform (53)
additional info: this server changes userPassword and nothing else, not cn
modifying entry "uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org"

A modify that asks for a password and something else is refused whole:a modify is atomic, and honouring half of it would report success for something nobody asked for.

Who can change what

request answer
no old password, or a bare replace: userPassword insufficientAccessRights
an old password that is not the current one unwillingToPerform
somebody else’s entry insufficientAccessRights, a password may be changed only by the person it belongs to
an anonymous connection insufficientAccessRights, an anonymous connection has not said who it is
somebody with no password at all — they can only have bound with a token unwillingToPerform: a bearer token is not a password, and does not set the first one. An administrator sets it in the configuration
somebody served from a users block unwillingToPerform: authnd reads those sources and does not write them
the file cannot be written other (80), the password could not be written; the reason is in the server’s output

The second-to-last, from the release binary, for dora, who comes from a SQLite database:

$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y dora.pwin -t dora.pwin -T dora.new
Result: Server is unwilling to perform (53)
Additional info: dora is served from a sqlite database, which this server reads and does not write

The person is matched by identity, not by DN: the session’s own name must be exactly the target’s, byte for byte, so a session bound as uid=Backup cannot change backup’s password even though the two DNs compare equal. That and the refusal of names that differ only by case are two controls that do not depend on each other.

Where the new password is written

Back into the file that declares the person, and nowhere else:

  • a user block with password_file has that file rewritten, keeping its owner and group where the process may, and its mode narrowed to at most 0600 — never widened;
  • a user block with password inline has the configuration file rewritten with the new value, keeping its comments, order and mode;
  • a user block with only an nt_hash is not given a password: that would change what can prove them, which is a change to the configuration.

Every write goes to a temporary file in the same directory, then a rename — so a full disk or a crash leaves the old password, not an empty file. That needs write access to the directory. Under the packaged unit,ProtectSystem=strict takes it away, and a change is refused like this:

$ ldapmodify -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -f safe.ldif
ldap_modify: Other (e.g., implementation specific) error (80)
additional info: the password could not be written
modifying entry "uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org"

with the reason in the server’s output:

changing the password for alice: etc/authnd/passwords/alice.pw: open etc/authnd/passwords/.hcldir-1822988247: permission denied

So keep the passwords in a directory of their own, writable by the service,and the configuration read-only to it — theReadWritePaths= drop-in.A person whose password is written inline would need /etc/authnd itself writable, which would also let the service rewrite its own configuration.

After a successful write, the configuration files are read again for theuser blocks only: an unrelated edit waiting on disk does not take effect halfway because somebody changed a password. Everything else still waits for a restart. The files are still read whole, though, so if one of them no longer loads, the password is written and the client is told the password was written but this server did not reload it — the running server keeps the old one until it is restarted.

item.title: A Kerberos realm for the same people
item.description:
kerberos {
 realm = "EXAMPLE.ORG" # required, upper case
 keytab = "/etc/authnd/krb5.keytab" # required; must hold krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG
 listen = "127.0.0.1:88" # the default; UDP and TCP both
 lifetime = "10h" # the default, MIT's
}

A kerberos block makes authnd a KDC as well as a directory, throughgo-authn/kdc: the same people are issued tickets instead of only being looked up. It answers on UDP and TCP at the same address, requires encrypted-timestamp pre-authentication, and issuesaes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 tickets only. lifetime is a Go duration("10h", "90m"). The directory and the realm are equals: if either stops,the process stops, because a server that kept answering LDAP after its KDC died would look healthy to everything that does not speak Kerberos.

Refused at startup:

$ authnd check cases/realm-lower.hcl
authnd: kerberos: realm "example.org" is not upper case: clients uppercase the realm they derive from a domain, and would then ask for a realm this server does not answer for

and likewise a realm with no name, no keytab, an address that does not parse,a lifetime Go cannot read, and a kerberos block beside an mfa block(below).

The keytab

The keytab holds the key authnd signs its own tickets with —krbtgt/REALM@REALM — and one key per service it issues tickets to. It is the same file those services read. The krbtgt password is never typed again, so make it random. With MIT’s ktutil (package krb5-user on Debian and Ubuntu; this recipe is the onedocs/install.md gives, and was not run for these pages):

printf 'addent -password -p krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG -k 1 -e aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96\n%s\nwkt /tmp/krb5.keytab\nquit\n' \
 "$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)" | ktutil
sudo install -o root -g authnd -m 0640 /tmp/krb5.keytab /etc/authnd/krb5.keytab
rm /tmp/krb5.keytab

Add a service’s key the same way (-p nfs/files.example.org@EXAMPLE.ORG), and give that service the same key in its own keytab. On macOS, Heimdal’sktutil -k <file> add -r -p <principal> -V 1 -e aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 writes a random key without a password at all. Either way, read the keytab back before starting (klist -k with MIT, ktutil -k <file> list with Heimdal):

$ ktutil -k etc/authnd/krb5.keytab list
etc/authnd/krb5.keytab:
Vno Type Principal Aliases
1 aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG

A keytab without krbtgt/REALM is refused by check and at start; seecheck.The keytab is read once, at start: replacing it takes a restart.

Who can be issued a ticket

A KDC must decrypt the client’s pre-authentication with that person’s long-term key, so it needs the person’s password, not only a way to check one. check says who can and who cannot, with the reason:

$ authnd check realm
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
bob the configuration file an NT hash account, uidObject uid
dora a sqlite database a password account, uidObject uid
eli a sqlite database an NT hash account, uidObject uid
GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS
staff alice and bob groupOfNames
alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
dora has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
eli has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
group staff has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid)
realm EXAMPLE.ORG on 127.0.0.1:18388 (udp and tcp), keytab etc/authnd/krb5.keytab
can be issued a ticket: alice and dora
CANNOT, whatever they type: bob and eli
a KDC must decrypt the pre-authentication with the person's key
bob and eli: an NT hash is only the RC4-HMAC key (RFC 4757), and this realm issues aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 alone, whose key is derived from the password itself
a bind carries a password
bob and eli cannot bind with a password: their sources hold only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against
no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served
the source has a ticket
a password (password, password_file, a SQL password column) yes
only an NT hash no: it is the RC4-HMAC key, and this realm issues AES only
only a password check (a users "ldap" directory behind this one) no: a source that only verifies a password cannot produce any key

For a directory behind this one, the last line of the realm part readsalice, bob, dora and eli: the source only verifies a password, so it cannot produce any key. That is structural rather than a matter of configuration,and finding it in check beats finding it from somebody whose kinit says their correct password is wrong.

kinit against it

A krb5.conf that names this KDC. ⛔ For MIT Kerberos the braces go on their own lines: its parser silently ignores a realm written on one line.

[libdefaults]
 default_realm = EXAMPLE.ORG
 dns_lookup_kdc = false
[realms]
 EXAMPLE.ORG = {
 kdc = 127.0.0.1:18388
 }

The same configuration served, and asked by macOS’s Heimdal kinit (--password-file reads the password from a file):

$ authnd --config realm
ldap on 127.0.0.1:3893, serving 4 people from the configuration file, then a sqlite database
realm EXAMPLE.ORG on 127.0.0.1:18388 (udp and tcp)
$ kinit --password-file=alice.pwin alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
$ klist
Credentials cache: FILE:ccache
Principal: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
Issued Expires Principal
Oct 26 12:42:50 2026 Oct 26 22:42:50 2026 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG
$ kinit --password-file=wrong.pwin alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
kinit: Password incorrect
$ kinit --password-file=bob.pwin bob@EXAMPLE.ORG
kinit: krb5_get_init_creds: Error from KDC: this realm holds no Kerberos key for that principal
$ kinit --password-file=dora.pwin zed@EXAMPLE.ORG
kinit: krb5_get_init_creds: Error from KDC: no such principal in this realm

The ticket lasts the default ten hours. bob typed the password their NT hash was computed from, and is still refused: the realm has no key for them. The KDC writes what it refused, with the Kerberos error code, to its output:

kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25)
kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25)
kerberos: the timestamp does not decrypt (client etype 18, our key type 18): error decrypting: integrity verification failed
kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication does not decrypt (code 24)
kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: this realm holds no Kerberos key for that principal (code 9)
kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: no such principal in this realm (code 6)

Pre-authentication required is the normal first round of a kinit: the client asks without pre-authentication and is told it is required, then asks again with it. alice’s successful kinit leaves only that line.

The realm says which names exist; the directory does not

An LDAP bind for a name nobody has is answered invalidCredentials, the same as a wrong password. The KDC answers no such principal in this realm (KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN, code 6), as Kerberos KDCs do. With akerberos block on an address others can reach, the list of names is therefore as guessable as it is from any KDC; listen defaults to loopback.

A password changed over LDAP

The KDC reads the same people the directory serves, so apassword changed over LDAP reaches the realm at once — the old one stops working for kinit the moment it stops working for a bind:

$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -t alice.pwin -T alice.new
$ kinit --password-file=alice.pwin alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
kinit: Password incorrect
$ kinit --password-file=alice.new alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
$

Not beside an mfa block 

$ authnd check cases/krb-mfa.hcl
authnd: kerberos and mfa together: the mfa block asks every bind for a password AND a code, and a kinit carries only the password -- this KDC has no second-factor pre-authentication, so a realm here would accept one factor where the mfa block demands two. Remove one of the blocks

RFC 4120’s encrypted-timestamp pre-authentication is keyed by the password alone. A second factor needs OTP pre-authentication (RFC 6560) inside FAST(RFC 6113), which this KDC does not implement. A realm here would hand out tickets on one factor to the people the mfa block says need two, and a ticket opens everything a bind does — so the choice is made closed: one or the other.

Ports

88 is privileged. Under the packaged unit, CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE covers it;a server run as an ordinary user wants a high port, as above, and akrb5.conf that names it.

item.title: A second factor, over a protocol with one field
item.description:
LDAP’s simple bind carries a name and a password and nothing else — no place for a code, no round trip to ask for one, and a client that speaks LDAP will not learn one. So the code goes on the end of the password, which is what appliances that do this do, and what people already know how to type:

password: hunter2314159
^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^
password the six digits on their phone
mfa {
 factors = 2
 distinct_kinds = true # two things they KNOW are not two factors
 # digits = 6, period = 30 (seconds) and window = 1 are the defaults
}

user "tess" {
 password_file = "/etc/authnd/passwords/tess.pw"
 totp_secret = "JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXPJBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP" # ⛔ this IS the second factor
}
key default
factors 2 1 is refused (a password and nothing else: remove the block, or ask for 2); above 2 is refused, since a bind carries a password and a code and no third thing
distinct_kinds false the factors must be of different kinds — what “two-factor” is normally taken to mean
digits 6 6 to 10 (RFC 4226)
period 30 seconds one code lasts
window 1 steps either side of now that are accepted, for clocks that differ. Each step is a step of somebody else’s guessing time: set it on purpose
readers false whether readers carry a code too. A service account has no phone; one that does gets a totp_secret in its reader block

The secret can equally come from a database column (the fifth) or an LDAP attribute (totp_attribute); see people.A totp_secret in a user or reader block under 128 bits (RFC 4226 R6)stops the server, naming the person, rather than failing every one of their logins later:

$ authnd check cases/shorttotp.hcl
authnd: user "alice": totp_secret is 80 bits, and RFC 4226 requires at least 128: enrol again with a longer secret

Who cannot bind under it 

$ authnd check mfa
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
tess the configuration file a password and a one-time-code secret account, uidObject uid
alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
tess has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
a bind carries a password with a 6-digit code after it, of two different kinds
alice has no second factor here, and cannot bind while one is required
cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

That is the question to ask before turning the block on.

What the binds look like

The same configuration served, tess’s code computed from their secret at the moment of the bind:

$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y tess.only
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y tess.both
dn:uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y tess.both
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y tess.badcode
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.code
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin
dn:cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org

tess.only is tess’s password with no code; tess.both the same password and the current code, sent twice; tess.badcode that password and 000000;alice.code alice’s password and six digits. The client is told one thing —invalid credentials — whichever half was wrong: which one is a fact about the account, and telling somebody who has proved nothing narrows their next guess. The server’s own output says which:

tess was refused: mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 0 answered: your password (knowledge): directory: wrong password; your authenticator app (possession): not looked at, since the password in front of it was wrong
tess was refused: mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 1 answered: your authenticator app (possession): totp: that code has already been used
tess was refused: mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 1 answered: your authenticator app (possession): totp: that code is not right
alice was refused: mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 1 answered: your authenticator app (possession): not available
your authenticator app: mfa: this factor cannot be asked here: totp: nobody enrolled an authenticator for this person

What follows from the one field

  • The split is by length. The last digits characters are the code. A password ending in digits is fine — that is why tess’s password alone was read as a wrong password followed by a code. A field no longer than a code is refused rather than guessed at, because a short password cannot be told apart from one.
  • Both halves are always checked. Returning early on a wrong password would say, in the time taken, which half was wrong.
  • A code is used once. It is valid for a whole step, so a server that accepts one twice accepts a replay; every step up to the last accepted one is refused, not merely the same one.
  • Guessing is limited per name, with go-authn/totp’s defaults: after five wrong codes in a row a person is refused for fifteen minutes, the right code included, and after a hundred they are locked out until authnd restarts. The counts are kept in memory, per process.
  • Only a code behind the right password is counted: otherwise anybody who knew a name could freeze its owner with five binds. Behind a wrong password the code is still computed, against nothing that remembers — the first line of the output above, not looked at.
  • A reader is counted under its DN as the configuration spells it, soCN=Reader gets no fresh budget of its own.
  • Nobody enrolled is not a wrong code. A person with no secret has answered nothing rather than answered wrongly, and the server’s output says nobody enrolled an authenticator for this person.

Not with a realm

A kerberos block and an mfa block in one configuration are refused: akinit proves the password and nothing else, and this KDC has no second-factor pre-authentication. Seethe realm.

Tokens, under the same policy

A token at the bind, with an oidc block,is counted by what its issuer says it checked — the amr claim. A token with no amr is one factor, and this policy refuses it.

item.title: A token at the bind, in a field that is not the password
item.description:
go-authn/oidc verifies a token into an identity. The obvious way to carry one to an LDAP server is the password field, and it works once and then stops: the password field is where themfa block takes the code off the end, and a token cannot be both.

So the token goes where the protocol has a place for it. A SASL bind’s credentials are an octet string of the mechanism’s own shape, and RFC 7628’sOAUTHBEARER shape is a GS2 header followed by key/value pairs, one of which is auth=Bearer <token>:

n,,^Aauth=Bearer eyJ…^A^A

The password field is left alone. On one listener, at the same time, a person can type a password with a code on the end and another can send a token.

oidc {
 issuer = "https://login.example.org/realms/staff" # the "iss" a token must carry, and where discovery starts
 audience = "ldap" # this server's client id at the provider

 # username_claim = "preferred_username" which claim names the person here
 # jwks_url = "…" skips discovery, for a provider that does not publish it
 # allow_plaintext = true only when TLS is terminated in front of this process
}

issuer and audience are required. Without username_claim, the name ispreferred_username, then email when email_verified is true, then sub.With the block, the root DSE advertises the mechanism:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -s base -b '' supportedSASLMechanisms
dn:
supportedSASLMechanisms: OAUTHBEARER

Without it, every SASL bind is answered authMethodNotSupported — not this way, which sends a client somewhere different from wrong password.

Discovery happens at startup

The provider’s discovery document and keys are read when the server starts,and by check. A provider that cannot be reached stops the server where somebody is watching, rather than refusing every bind later:

$ authnd check cases/oidc.hcl
authnd: oidc "https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff": oidc: reading https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff/.well-known/openid-configuration: Get "https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff/.well-known/openid-configuration": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect: connection refused

An issuer that is not https is refused, except on loopback:

$ authnd check cases/oidc-http.hcl
authnd: oidc "http://login.example.org/realms/staff": oidc: http://login.example.org/realms/staff is not https: the key set decides every signature, and over cleartext so does anybody on the way

How many factors is a token?

Whatever the issuer says it checked, and nothing more. A token carries RFC 8176’s amr, the methods the provider used. That is the only evidence there is, so it is what the mfa policy counts, by kind:

amr method kind
pwd, pin, kba, mca knowledge
otp, hwk, swk, sms, tel, sc, pop, user, wia, mfa possession
fpt, face, iris, retina, vbm, geo inherence
anything else unknown, which never satisfies distinct_kinds
no amr at all one factor, possession — the token itself

Two methods of one kind are one factor. The alternative would be this server inventing a second factor nobody performed; and a server that believes the issuer about who this is has no separate ground for disbelieving it abouthow it checked.

With an mfa block, check says it:

$ authnd check sasl
ldaps://127.0.0.1:3636, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
tess the configuration file a password and a one-time-code secret account, uidObject uid
alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
tess has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
a bind carries a password with a 6-digit code after it, of two different kinds
or a token from http://127.0.0.1:18481, over SASL OAUTHBEARER over TLS
a token counts for the factors its amr claim names, so one with no amr is refused by this policy
alice has no second factor here, so a password cannot satisfy this policy; a token whose amr names two kinds still can
no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

alice has no totp_secret, so a password with a code can never be enough for them; a token whose amr names two kinds can, as the first bind below shows.

What the binds look like

The issuer here is a small test provider on loopback, and oidctool a test client written for these pages: it signs a token for the name given, with the amr given, sends it in an OAUTHBEARER bind (with an authzid when a fifth argument names one), and prints the bind’s result code and the server’s SASL credentials. These transcripts, and the server lines below, were printed by the v0.10.0 release binary and not run again, since oidctool is part of no release. Against the configuration above, over ldaps://:

$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 0, serverSaslCreds
$ ./oidctool alice '' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 49
$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","kba"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 49
$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls tess
bind result 14, serverSaslCreds {"status":"insufficient_scope","openid-configuration":"http://127.0.0.1:18481/.well-known/openid-configuration"}
$ ./oidctool zed '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 14, serverSaslCreds {"status":"invalid_token","openid-configuration":"http://127.0.0.1:18481/.well-known/openid-configuration"}

0 is success, 49 invalidCredentials, 14 saslBindInProgress. A["pwd","kba"] token names two methods of one kind, so it counts once. And to the same configuration without cert_file and key_file, on a plaintext listener:

$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3893 clear
bind result 13

13 is confidentialityRequired: a token is not taken over a connection that is not encrypted.

What the server wrote for the four binds over ldaps:// that were refused:

alice was refused: mfa: the policy needs 2 factor(s) and 1 were offered
alice was refused: mfa: the policy needs 2 factor(s) and 1 were offered
alice was refused: the token is for "alice" and asks to act as "tess"; this server does not delegate
zed was refused: the token verified, and no source here publishes anybody by that name

and for the plaintext one:

a token was refused: OAUTHBEARER was offered over a connection that is not encrypted, and allow_plaintext is not set

A successful OAUTHBEARER bind leaves the connection bound asuid=<name>,ou=people,<base_dn>, spelled as every other entry is.

What it refuses

  • A token in the clear. A bearer token needs no other half: whoever reads it off the wire is that person until it expires. allow_plaintext = true exists for a deployment that terminates TLS in front of this process, andcheck then says a token may cross this socket in the clear.
  • A request to be somebody else. The GS2 header may name an authzid. A token for alice carrying a request to act as tess is refused, not quietly treated as either.
  • A token for somebody no source here publishes. The client is told onlyinvalid_token; which names exist is not something to hand out one guess at a time. The reason is in the server’s output.
  • Channel binding. A GS2 header with p= — the client insists on channel binding — is refused: this server does not do it, and accepting the header while binding nothing would let the client believe the channel was checked.
  • A mechanism this server does not speak, with authMethodNotSupported.

A refusal of the token itself is RFC 7628 §3.2.3’s: a JSON error carryingopenid-configuration, returned as saslBindInProgress so the client can send the ^A that ends the exchange. A token that verifies but does not satisfy the mfa policy is answered plainly invalidCredentials, as the second and third binds above show.

A token does not set a password

A person who has only ever signed in with a token cannot use that session to give themselves a first password, and a person who has one must still send it to change it. See changing a password.

item.title: Running it: signals, restarts and what it says
item.description:
It reads everything once

The configuration files, every source behind them, the TLS certificate and the keytab are read at start. There is no reload, and the packaged unit has no ExecReload=. After changing any of them:

sudo -u authnd authnd check /etc/authnd
sudo systemctl restart authnd

The one thing applied while it runs is apassword a person changes through authnd,which re-reads the user blocks and nothing else.

That includes the groups. A search asks no database anything, so a change to a group in a database is picked up by a restart, and a database that breaks while authnd runs changes no answer. (Before v0.13.4 every search queried the groups again — 4.13 s a search over 200 groups on SQLite — and a query that failed dropped the group from an answer that still said Success.) A source that cannot be read at start, such as a groups query that does not run or one of several databases being down, refuses the start and check, naming the source and the group. An entry too large for one LDAP message (about 3 MiB, which one 10 MB attribute value is enough to reach) is not published, and is said at start and by check, like an entry that fails the schema.

Signals

signal what happens
SIGTERM, SIGINT it prints stopping, closes the listeners and every established connection, stops the realm, closes the sources, and exits 0 once the server has really finished
SIGHUP it is caught and logged, and authnd stays up without reloading anything 
$ authnd --config etc/authnd
ldap on 127.0.0.1:3893, serving 4 people from the configuration file, then a sqlite database
hangup: authnd does not reload; restart it to apply a changed configuration, certificate or keytab
alice's password change was refused: the old password did not verify: directory: wrong password
alice changed their own password
stopping

That is one run: a kill -HUP, two attempts to change a password (the first refused, the second accepted), then a kill -TERM.The process was still there after the SIGHUP.

A SIGHUP used to kill authnd — Go’s default for a signal nobody handles— and systemd counts death by SIGHUP as a clean exit, soRestart=on-failure did not start it again: one kill -HUP or one logrotatepostrotate took a directory down for good. It is caught now so that the habit is harmless, and the line says what to do instead.

Closing established connections, not only the listener, is deliberate: a server that stopped accepting and left its open connections answering would look stopped and not be, which is the restart that does not take.

What it writes

Everything goes to standard output, which under systemd is the journal(journalctl -u authnd):

  • at start, where it listens and whom it serves — ldap on …, ldaps on … or ldap+starttls on …, then realm EXAMPLE.ORG on … (udp and tcp) with akerberos block;
  • every refused bind under an mfa block, every refused token, every refused or completed password change, with the reason — which the client is never told; see the second factor and tokens;
  • every request the KDC refuses, prefixed kerberos:, with the Kerberos error code; see the realm;
  • the LDAP library’s own log, in slog text form, at level info.

A plain wrong password on a simple bind, with no mfa block, is answeredinvalidCredentials and not logged by authnd itself.

When it does not start

A refusal is one line on standard error, prefixed authnd:, and exit status 1; under the unit, Restart=on-failure then tries again every five seconds and the line is in the journal each time. Everything check refuses is refused here too, and the one thing only the server finds is an address it cannot listen on — seecheck.The LDAP listener, the certificate and the realm are all opened before the first line is printed, so a server that cannot start prints only the refusal. Here a second instance meets the first one’s Kerberos port:

$ authnd --config cases/realm2
authnd: kerberos udp 127.0.0.1:18388: listen udp 127.0.0.1:18388: bind: address already in use

The ldap on … line, and realm … on … after it, mean both halves are listening.

Telling that it is up

There is no health endpoint and no metrics. What there is:

  • the process and its exit status — under systemd, systemctl is-active authnd. If the LDAP listener or the realm stops of its own accord, the whole process ends with that error, so a live process is one whose two halves both answer;
  • the root DSE, which answers an anonymous client and says which version it is talking to:
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -s base -b '' '+' '*'
dn:
objectClass: top
objectClass: OpenLDAProotDSE
supportedLDAPVersion: 3
namingContexts: dc=example,dc=org
supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.3
supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.1
supportedControl: 1.2.840.113556.1.4.319
supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.1
supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.2
supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.1
supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.3
subschemaSubentry: cn=Subschema
vendorName: go-authn/authnd
vendorVersion: v0.13.0

On a StartTLS listener that query needs -ZZ. A probe that proves more — that a source still answers — is a bind as a person or a reader kept for the purpose; with ausers "ldap" block, that bind reaches the directory behind this one.

What lives where, and what a restart loses

configuration, passwords, DSN, certificate, keytab the files the configuration names; nothing is copied
a SQLite database wherever its DSN says; /var/lib/authnd under the unit
second-factor counts and lockouts memory only: a restart forgets them, including a person locked out after a hundred wrong codes
used one-time codes memory only
